questions.question: What is a key difference between an Observable and a Promise?
options: A Promise can emit multiple values over time; an Observable cannot
An Observable is lazy and only starts executing when subscribed to; a Promise starts eagerly
Observables cannot be used with HTTP requests
questions.explanation: Observables don't do anything until subscribe() is called, and they can emit zero, one, or many values over time — unlike a Promise, which starts immediately and resolves once.

questions.question: In a type-ahead search, why is `switchMap` preferred over `mergeMap`?
options: switchMap cancels the previous in-flight request when a new value arrives, preventing a stale response from overwriting a newer one
There is no difference between them
questions.explanation: switchMap switches to the latest inner Observable and unsubscribes from the previous one, which is exactly what's needed to avoid race conditions in search-as-you-type.

questions.question: What does `combineLatest([a$, b$])` do?
options: Waits for both to complete, then emits once
Emits a new combined value whenever either source observable emits, using each one's latest value
Merges the two streams into one without pairing values
questions.explanation: combineLatest re-emits an array of the latest values whenever any one of its source observables produces a new value.

questions.question: Why use `takeUntilDestroyed()` when subscribing manually inside a component class?
options: It automatically unsubscribes when the component is destroyed, preventing memory leaks
It replaces the need for the async pipe entirely
It only works with HttpClient observables
questions.explanation: takeUntilDestroyed() ties the subscription's lifetime to the component's lifecycle so it's cleaned up automatically, avoiding leaks from forgotten manual unsubscribes.
